name: Glucose, fasting
low: Low glucose can cause shakiness, sweating or confusion. Discuss with a clinician, especially if you take diabetes medicine.
high: Fasting glucose of 100–125 mg/dL is in the prediabetes range; 126 mg/dL or more on two tests is in the diabetes range (ADA). Confirm with A1c or a repeat test.

name: Hemoglobin A1c
high: A1c of 5.7–6.4% is the prediabetes range; 6.5% or more is the diabetes range (ADA). Anemia and some hemoglobin variants can skew A1c.

name: Total cholesterol
high: Total cholesterol includes LDL, HDL and other particles. LDL, non-HDL cholesterol and your overall risk matter more than the total.

name: LDL cholesterol
high: Higher LDL raises the risk of plaque build-up. An LDL of 190 mg/dL or more can signal an inherited condition and usually warrants treatment discussion.

name: HDL cholesterol
low: Low HDL is linked with higher heart risk. Activity, not smoking and weight loss can raise it.

name: Triglycerides
high: Triglycerides rise after meals, with alcohol, excess sugar, uncontrolled diabetes and some medicines. Very high levels (500+) can inflame the pancreas.

name: Apolipoprotein B
high: US guidelines treat ApoB of 130 mg/dL or more as a risk-enhancing factor. European guidelines set lower goals for higher-risk people.

name: Lipoprotein(a)
high: Lp(a) is mostly inherited. 50 mg/dL or more is a risk-enhancing factor; focus on controlling other risks. Check whether your report uses mg/dL or nmol/L.

name: Hemoglobin
low: Low hemoglobin means anemia. Common causes are iron deficiency, blood loss, B12 or folate deficiency and chronic illness.
high: High hemoglobin can come from dehydration, smoking, living at altitude, testosterone therapy or, rarely, bone-marrow conditions.

name: Hematocrit
low: Low hematocrit usually moves with low hemoglobin and suggests anemia.
high: High hematocrit can reflect dehydration or more red cells than usual.

name: White blood cells
low: Low white cells can follow viral infections or some medicines; persistent lows need follow-up.
high: High white cells often reflect infection, inflammation, stress, smoking or steroid medicines.

name: Platelets
low: Low platelets can increase bruising and bleeding. Causes include viral infections, medicines and liver disease.
high: High platelets often follow inflammation, iron deficiency or recent infection.

name: Creatinine
low: Low creatinine usually reflects lower muscle mass and is rarely a concern.
high: High creatinine can mean reduced kidney filtering, dehydration, high muscle mass, creatine supplements or a large meat meal.

name: eGFR
low: An eGFR below 60 for three months or more is consistent with chronic kidney disease. 60–89 alone is common with age and isn't CKD without other signs of kidney damage.

name: BUN (urea nitrogen)
low: Low BUN can reflect low protein intake or liver disease.
high: High BUN can reflect dehydration, high protein intake, bleeding in the gut or reduced kidney function.

name: ALT
high: Raised ALT points to liver irritation: fatty liver, alcohol, medicines, viral hepatitis or recent intense exercise are common causes.

name: AST
high: AST is found in liver and muscle, so heavy exercise as well as liver conditions can raise it.

name: Sodium
low: Low sodium can follow excess water intake, diuretics, some antidepressants or heart, liver and kidney conditions.
high: High sodium usually reflects dehydration.

name: Potassium
low: Low potassium can follow vomiting, diarrhea or diuretics and can affect heart rhythm.
high: A high result is often caused by the blood draw itself and is usually repeated, but true high potassium affects heart rhythm and needs prompt attention.

name: Calcium
low: Low calcium is often due to low albumin; check albumin on the same report. Low vitamin D can also contribute.
high: High calcium can come from overactive parathyroid glands, excess supplements or other conditions and deserves follow-up.

name: TSH
low: Low TSH suggests an overactive thyroid or too much thyroid medicine.
high: High TSH suggests an underactive thyroid; it's usually rechecked with free T4.

name: Free T4
low: Low free T4 with high TSH indicates an underactive thyroid.
high: High free T4 with low TSH indicates an overactive thyroid.

name: Vitamin D, 25-hydroxy
low: Below 12 ng/mL is deficient and 12–19 ng/mL is inadequate for bone health (NIH ODS).
high: Above 50 ng/mL offers no proven extra benefit and very high levels can be harmful.

name: Ferritin
low: Low ferritin means depleted iron stores, even before anemia appears.
high: High ferritin often reflects inflammation, liver disease or alcohol; iron overload is checked with transferrin saturation.

name: Iron, serum
low: Low serum iron can reflect deficiency or inflammation; ferritin and transferrin saturation tell them apart.
high: High serum iron can follow supplements or iron overload.

name: Vitamin B12
low: Low B12 can cause anemia and nerve symptoms. Results around 200–300 pg/mL are often checked with methylmalonic acid.
high: High B12 usually reflects supplements.

name: hs-CRP
high: Above 3 mg/L suggests higher cardiovascular risk if you were well when tested. Over 10 mg/L usually means a recent infection or injury.

name: Testosterone, total
low: A single low value isn't a diagnosis. Guidelines call for a repeat early-morning test and symptoms.
high: High testosterone in women can point to PCOS or other conditions; in men it usually reflects testosterone use.

name: PSA
high: PSA rises with age, prostate enlargement, infection and recent ejaculation or cycling. Follow-up is usually a repeat test first.

name: Uric acid
low: Low uric acid is rarely a concern.
high: Uric acid above about 6.8 mg/dL can form crystals and trigger gout.
